name: Tokio TCP echo server (Boost.Redis echo benchmark, vs libuv)
baseline: libuv TCP echo server (C, epoll event loop, libuv docs tcp-echo-server example); the table also holds a Boost.Asio C++20 coroutine echo server that is slightly faster than Tokio
workload: TCP echo server serving 1000 concurrent client connections on localhost (the Boost.Redis echo_server_client driver, benchmarks.tex comment 'time ./echo_server_client 1000 5000'); metric is the total wall-clock seconds the client run took against each server, one server per language/library, each written from that library's own docs example.
claimed_speedup: Tokio 30.7 s vs libuv 43.6 s for the same echo run (about 1.42x less wall time, derived from page data). Boost.Asio (C++) 29.5 s is about 4% faster than Tokio (derived from page data). Go 35.6 s and Node.js 74.2 s are in the same table.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Tokio server uses #[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")] with tokio 1 (features full) from benchmarks/rust/echo_server_direct; cargo profile not stated. Asio client/server built with CMake C++20 (benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt); libuv build flags not stated.
stars_or_usage: 33.4k stars (tokio); suite repo boostorg/redis has 282 stars
tradeoffs: Rust async needs the Tokio runtime and a Rust toolchain; the benchmark deliberately uses the single-threaded Tokio runtime to match the single-threaded libuv loop. Calling it from C++ needs FFI or a separate process.
caveats: Numbers are the pgfplots source (benchmarks.tex) of the chart that the Boost.Redis doc page 'Echo server benchmark' shows; the rendered chart image itself was not viewed. Machine is only described as 'my machine' (localhost latency 0.07 ms): no CPU model, no OS, no compiler or Rust/Go versions, no flags, one run, no variance. The author is the Boost.Redis (C++) author, not a maintainer of the tested runtime. The libuv server is the unmodified libuv docs tcp-echo-server example (malloc of a read buffer and of a write request for every message), so it is an untuned C baseline. The C++ Boost.Asio coroutine server in the same table is the fastest entry (29.5 s), so this is not a win over the best C++ result. All servers are single-threaded (Asio io_context with an unsafe-IO hint, Tokio current_thread runtime, Go GOMAXPROCS(1), one libuv loop). The doc page says the author expected libuv to perform like Asio and Tokio and was surprised by the Go result; it offers no explanation of the gap. The runtime-level win is only over libuv (untuned C example); Tokio loses to Boost.Asio in the same suite.
found_via: WebSearch: 'tokio vs boost asio benchmark echo server rust faster than C++ github' surfaced the Boost.Redis benchmark page; opened github.com/boostorg/redis benchmarks directory, benchmarks.tex, doc/modules/ROOT/pages/benchmarks.adoc and the rust/libuv/go/asio sources via raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: Embassy (async Rust executor) vs FreeRTOS
baseline: FreeRTOS (C RTOS, used through the CMSIS-RTOS v2 wrapper in an STM32CubeIDE project) on an STM32F446ZE
workload: README claim that async tasks make a traditional RTOS with kernel context switching unnecessary; the linked Tweede Golf 'async vs RTOS showdown' implements the same firmware in Embassy and FreeRTOS on a NUCLEO-F446ZE and (per search-result summaries, blog unreachable) compares interrupt latency, program size and static RAM.
claimed_speedup: README quote: 'It obsoletes the need for a traditional RTOS with kernel context switching, and is faster and smaller than one!' No figures appear on any page that was opened; the blog post that carries them (tweedegolf.nl, async-rust-vs-rtos-showdown) could not be reached from this environment.
compiler_and_flags: Rust project (rust/Cargo.toml): opt-level = 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1, embassy from git master of early 2022, nightly features. C project: STM32CubeIDE 1.8.0 .cproject, Release configuration with C optimization -O3 (C++ option -Os), arm-none-eabi toolchain; compiler versions not stated.
tradeoffs: Cooperative async tasks, not preemptive threads: a task that does not yield blocks the others, and priorities work through multiple executors/interrupts. Needs Rust nightly features in the 2022 snapshot; no C++ API.
caveats: Tier D because no number could be read from an opened page; tier could rise to A if the blog's figures are reachable (benchmark code, flags and MCU are public). Search-result summaries of the blog disagree on interrupt latency (one says FreeRTOS wins interrupt latency, another says Embassy wins most metrics but FreeRTOS is slightly faster from interrupt end to thread wake-up) and Hacker News commenters said worst-case latency was not measured. The showdown repo is a Feb 2022 snapshot (3 commits) built on Embassy master of that date, so the result predates four years of Embassy and FreeRTOS changes. A cooperative executor versus a preemptive RTOS is not a like-for-like scheduling comparison. The only repo claim is a README sentence.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Embassy async rust vs FreeRTOS benchmark latency context switch'; opened github.com/embassy-rs/embassy README, github.com/tweedegolf/async-rtos-showdown (README, rust/Cargo.toml, c/.cproject, commits).
why_faster: README: async tasks compile into cooperatively scheduled state machines that share one stack, need no per-task stack sizing and no dynamic allocation, so no kernel context switch is paid.

name: Rayon vs OpenMP (CMU 15-618 project)
baseline: C++ with OpenMP (and GNU parallel-mode sort) for Mandelbrot, matrix multiplication, sorting and reduction; C++ compiled with GCC per the report
workload: Four shared-memory benchmarks written in Rust+Rayon and C++/OpenMP: Mandelbrot (2048 to 8192 square images), matrix multiplication (1024 and 2048 square), stable and unstable sort of 1M, 10M and 100M random elements (Rayon par_sort vs GNU parallel sort), and sum/sum-of-squares reduction over 500M, 1B and 2B f64; best of three runs, thread counts swept.
claimed_speedup: Mixed result, graphs only. Report: Rayon faster than OpenMP for 2048x2048 matrix multiply at every thread count and for stable (merge) sort at higher thread counts; C++ faster for 1024x1024 matmul, for unstable sort at large sizes, for Mandelbrot (Rust within 1% in the multithreaded case) and for reduction. Only quoted timings: serial Mandelbrot 4096x4096 view 1, Rust 19319.043 ms vs C++ 18813.754 ms before the fix and 18758.684 ms after removing the Complex32 overhead.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (report mentions GCC for the C++ side and Clang/LLVM for the Rust side; no optimization flags or versions; Rayon 1.0.3).
tradeoffs: Rayon work stealing adapts to uneven work but pays split and steal overhead; the report finds OpenMP static scheduling faster on reductions and Mandelbrot. Rust refuses to compile unsafe sharing between threads.
caveats: Student course project: results are graphs inside a PDF, no hardware or compiler flags stated, no license file. The Rayon matmul win comes from Rust not vectorizing the inner loop (C++ vectorized it and hit a compute limit at 8 threads) and from par_chunks removing fork-join overhead, so it is not evidence that Rayon is the better scheduler. The sort comparison pits Rust's merge sort and pdqsort-based sort against GNU parallel sort, so the algorithms differ. Rayon 1.0.3 era (2018-2019).
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/rayon and github.com/topics/openmp?l=rust (repo description 'Comparison of Multi-threading between C++ and Rust (OpenMP vs Rayon)'); opened repo README, project_docs/15618-Project-Final.pdf and commits.
why_faster: Report: Rayon work stealing balances load and its merge sort was tuned (three merge variants benchmarked); for 2048x2048 matmul the unvectorized Rust inner loop keeps scaling longer and par_chunks avoids fork-join overhead.
